problems.title: Energy retrofit contractors and building owners cannot independently verify savings calculations, causing payment disputes
problems.description: After an energy retrofit is installed under a performance-based contract, the contractor and building owner must agree on the actual energy savings delivered. Both parties typically perform their own calculations using the same meter data but different baseline models, weather normalization methods, and data sources. Because no shared tamper-evident baseline exists and no standard machine-readable format is agreed at contract start, the calculations frequently diverge. Resolving the dispute requires either protracted negotiation or engaging an expensive third-party M&V verifier, delaying final payment by weeks to months.

actors.organizationType: Energy Service Company or specialist retrofit contractor

jobs.statement: Verify that an installed energy retrofit delivered the contractually agreed performance outcome before releasing final payment.
Demonstrate to a building owner that the installed retrofit measures delivered the contractually defined energy savings, using meter data adjusted for occupancy and weather.

workflowSummary.name: Energy Retrofit Performance Measurement & Verification (M&V) Settlement
workflowSummary.trigger: Contractor submits performance claim at a contractual milestone date, typically 12 months after retrofit installation.
workflowSummary.goal: Both parties agree on actual energy savings achieved and contractor receives agreed performance-based payment.

steps.action: Export metered energy consumption data from building energy management system (BEMS) or smart meters for the measurement period.
Apply weather normalization (heating degree days) to adjust measured consumption for climate differences between baseline and measurement period.
steps.input: Metered data, weather data (external weather service), baseline model
steps.frictionNotes: Contractor and building owner may use different weather data sources or degree-day calculation methods, producing different normalization results.

steps.action: Compare normalized consumption against the agreed pre-retrofit baseline to calculate claimed energy savings.
steps.input: Normalized measurement period data, baseline data
steps.output: Claimed savings figure and performance report

steps.action: Submit performance report and payment claim to building owner.
Review submitted performance report. Attempt to verify claimed savings against own meter data and baseline understanding.
steps.input: Contractor performance report, own meter data
steps.output: Owner's own verification calculation or questions
steps.frictionNotes: Building owner often cannot reproduce contractor's calculation because baseline methodology, weather data source, and normalization formula are not standardized or shared in machine-readable form.

steps.action: Request clarification or dispute the savings claim.
steps.input: Discrepancy found between own calculation and contractor claim
steps.frictionNotes: Dispute is common when occupancy, process, or weather changed significantly during measurement period. Resolving requires iterative back-and-forth.

steps.action: If dispute cannot be resolved bilaterally, independent M&V verifier is engaged. Verifier collects data from both parties, applies agreed IPMVP option, and issues binding report.
steps.input: Data from contractor and building owner, site visit if required
steps.frictionNotes: Engagements cost EUR 5,000–50,000+. Adds weeks to months of delay. Often the verifier must reconstruct a baseline that was not properly documented at contract start.

steps.action: Accept M&V report finding and authorize payment, or continue to dispute through contract arbitration.
steps.output: Payment authorization or escalation to arbitration

handoffs.frictionNotes: Handoff crosses organizational boundary. Data is in PDF/Word, not machine-readable. Building owner must re-enter data to verify.

handoffs.delay: 2–6 weeks to engage and mobilize verifier

frictions.description: Baseline data typically exists in a format (Excel, PDF) that requires manual re-entry by the building owner to verify contractor calculations.
No standard tamper-evident mechanism for the pre-retrofit baseline. Both parties may believe their version is correct.
Engaging an independent M&V verifier takes 4–12 weeks and EUR 5,000–50,000+, creating a major delay and cost overhang.
Weather normalization uses different data sources (weather stations, degree-day providers) and methods, producing results that diverge across systems.

workarounds.description: Building owners hire an independent M&V verifier (IPMVP-certified engineer) to adjudicate disputes.
workarounds.cost: EUR 5,000–50,000 per engagement plus 4–12 weeks delay
workarounds.limitations: Adds significant time and cost. Does not prevent the dispute from arising in the first place. Many SME building owners cannot afford this.

workarounds.description: Some parties agree to a simplified deemed savings approach (kWh per installed unit), avoiding M&V altogether but sacrificing accuracy.
workarounds.method: Deemed savings tables from industry bodies
workarounds.limitations: Does not reflect actual building performance. Inaccurate for complex retrofits or buildings with variable occupancy.

contexts: Energy Performance Contracts (EPCs) with performance-based payment obligations
Post-retrofit M&V period, typically 1–3 years after installation
Buildings with variable occupancy or processes (hospitals, factories, retail) where baseline adjustment is most contested

evidence.summary: Reconstructed from HeatProof (idea-433) dossier — the idea explicitly targets M&V dispute in energy performance contracts. Dossier references that EPCs with verified performance are an EU policy objective under the Energy Efficiency Directive. Real user interviews with building owners and ESCOs needed.

counterEvidence.summary: Large sophisticated building owners (major commercial real estate portfolios, municipalities with dedicated energy teams) may already have internal capacity to perform M&V, reducing the severity of this problem for that segment. The problem may be most acute for SME building owners or smaller ESCOs.

Where IPMVP Option A (stipulated measurement) is contractually agreed from the start, the scope of what must be verified is pre-limited, reducing dispute potential. If most contracts already use simplified stipulated approaches, the full dispute workflow may be rarer than assumed.

currentWorkarounds: Hire independent M&V verifier (IPMVP-certified engineer) — costs EUR 5,000–50,000 and 4–12 weeks
Use deemed savings tables (kWh per installed unit) — simpler but inaccurate for complex retrofits
Bilateral negotiation with manual Excel models from both parties
consequences: Payment delayed weeks to months pending dispute resolution
Building owner bears M&V verification cost on top of retrofit cost
M&V dispute cost reduces effective ROI of retrofit for both parties
Disputes deter smaller ESCOs from offering performance-based contracts
desiredOutcomes: Both parties can independently reproduce the verified savings calculation from shared, tamper-evident source data
Minimize time and cost to reach agreed performance settlement
Eliminate or dramatically reduce the need for third-party M&V verification in standard cases
researchGaps: What share of EPCs result in M&V disputes vs. smooth settlement?
What is the typical cost and duration of dispute resolution?
Are large sophisticated buyers already well-served by existing M&V software?
What does current adoption of IPMVP-certified M&V software look like?

linkedIdeas.residualProblem: HeatProof addresses the verification and dispute step by providing shared tamper-evident baseline and weather normalization infrastructure. However, it does not address the upstream problem that baseline methodology must still be agreed at contract start. If parties use different IPMVP options at contract negotiation, disagreement on scope will persist even with shared data infrastructure.

problems.title: Industrial sites cannot independently verify their grid flexibility performance because SCADA data and grid operator settlement data use incompatible identifiers and timestamps
problems.description: Industrial sites participating in grid flexibility markets (demand response, balancing mechanism) deliver MW load reductions on instruction from aggregators. Payment is performance-based. However, the site's SCADA system logs power consumption using site-internal meter IDs and local timestamps, while the grid operator measures delivered response using half-hourly settlement periods and Meter Point Reference Numbers (MPRNs/MPANs). The aggregator must manually map between these two incompatible identifier schemes every settlement cycle. Industrial sites receive only a summary statement from the aggregator and cannot access raw grid operator data, leaving them unable to independently verify their payment. Disputes require weeks to resolve.

actors.role: Energy Manager / Flexibility Coordinator at Industrial Site
actors.organizationType: Energy-intensive industrial manufacturer (steel, cement, chemicals, paper, etc.)

actors.role: Flexibility Aggregator / Virtual Power Plant Operator
actors.organizationType: Specialized energy aggregation company or utility subsidiary

jobs.statement: Prove the actual megawatt-hour flexibility response delivered during a grid flexibility event matches what the aggregator will use for settlement payment.
Distribute performance-based payments accurately across enrolled flexibility participants after reconciling each site's delivered response against grid operator settlement data.

workflowSummary.name: Industrial Grid Flexibility Event Response & Settlement Reconciliation
workflowSummary.trigger: Grid operator calls a flexibility event (e.g. Balancing Mechanism instruction, demand response call, capacity market delivery obligation).
workflowSummary.goal: Industrial site receives accurate performance-based payment for flexible load reduction delivered during the event.

steps.action: Receive flexibility event instruction from grid operator. Dispatch instruction to enrolled industrial sites.
steps.input: Grid operator event signal (time, volume, duration)

steps.action: Receive dispatch instruction. Execute load curtailment or shift on site (e.g. pause furnace, delay compressor, adjust HVAC).
Site SCADA automatically logs power demand at 1-minute or 30-minute intervals during and after event.
steps.output: SCADA event log with timestamps and MW readings
steps.frictionNotes: SCADA timestamps may be in local time with DST ambiguity. Meter resolution (1-min vs 30-min) may differ from grid operator's settlement resolution.

steps.action: Receive settlement data from grid operator showing measured delivered response volume per participant.
steps.system: Grid operator portal (e.g. National Grid ESO, RTE, TenneT)

steps.action: Attempt to reconcile grid operator settlement data against site-reported SCADA data to verify delivered MW response per site.
steps.input: Grid operator settlement data, site SCADA export
steps.output: Reconciled or disputed site performance figures
steps.frictionNotes: Key friction point: site SCADA uses site-specific meter IDs; grid operator uses its own meter point reference numbers (MPRNs/MPANs). Timestamps differ. Must manually map between identifiers. 30-minute settlement period may not align with SCADA minute-by-minute log.

steps.action: Calculate payment for each site based on reconciled delivered volume × price. Apply performance haircuts for sites that under-delivered.
steps.input: Reconciled performance data, price from grid operator
steps.output: Site payment calculations with haircuts applied

steps.action: Receive settlement statement from aggregator. Verify that aggregator's reported MW response matches own SCADA log.
steps.system: Excel / manual review of SCADA export
steps.frictionNotes: Site operator often cannot independently reproduce aggregator's calculation because the grid operator's settlement data is not directly shared with the industrial site — only with the aggregator.

steps.action: If discrepancy found, raise dispute with aggregator. Aggregator must then re-verify with grid operator data.
steps.input: Site SCADA log, aggregator settlement statement
steps.frictionNotes: Dispute resolution may take weeks. Industrial sites often lack leverage to dispute aggregators who control their access to the market.

handoffs.frictionNotes: Data arrives in grid operator format, not site SCADA format. Identifier mapping required.
Industrial site receives summary statement only, not raw grid operator data, limiting its ability to independently verify.

frictions.description: Site SCADA meter IDs do not match grid operator Meter Point Reference Numbers (MPRNs). Manual mapping required every settlement cycle.
SCADA logs and grid operator settlement data use different timestamp granularities and formats, requiring manual alignment.
Industrial sites do not have direct access to grid operator settlement data — only aggregator does. Site cannot independently verify its own performance as measured by the grid operator.
Industrial site must trust aggregator's reconciliation. No independent verification mechanism exists for the site unless it disputes.

workarounds.description: Aggregators build proprietary reconciliation tools internally that map site IDs to grid operator references and normalize timestamps.
workarounds.method: Custom internal tool or Excel macro
workarounds.limitations: Each aggregator recreates the same tool independently. Not standardized across markets. Errors in ID mapping cause payment disputes.

workarounds.description: Industrial sites export their SCADA data manually and compare it to their payment statement in a spreadsheet to look for anomalies.
workarounds.limitations: Site still cannot access raw grid operator data to confirm its measurement, only its own SCADA reading.

contexts: Demand response / flexibility markets in European electricity systems (UK BM, German FCR/aFRR, French NEBEF, etc.)
Sites with high-resolution SCADA (1-minute data) vs. 30-minute grid settlement

evidence.summary: Reconstructed from FlexCovenant (idea-434) dossier. The identifier-mismatch problem is structurally inherent in the architecture of European flexibility markets, where SCADA systems predated smart meter standardization. Direct interviews with flexibility aggregators and industrial energy managers needed.

counterEvidence.summary: Some markets (UK half-hourly settlement reform, EU Smart Meter rollout) are gradually standardizing meter data formats, which could reduce the identifier mismatch problem over time if widely adopted.
Large sophisticated aggregators operating at scale may already have mature automated reconciliation tools, leaving only smaller aggregators or newer market entrants as the addressable pain point.

currentWorkarounds: Aggregators build proprietary internal reconciliation tools (Excel macros or custom software) to map IDs and normalize timestamps
Industrial sites manually export SCADA data and compare against summary statements in Excel — cannot fully verify
Sites accept occasional haircuts rather than invest time in dispute resolution
consequences: Sites receive incorrect (haircut) payments without knowing if it reflects under-performance or identifier/timing mismatch
Dispute resolution takes weeks; sites lack leverage against aggregators who control market access
Aggregators invest significant internal engineering time recreating identifier-mapping tools for each market
Systematic under-payment due to undetected identifier errors depresses industrial participation in flexibility markets
desiredOutcomes: Industrial site can independently verify, immediately after a flexibility event, that its SCADA-measured response matches the grid operator's recorded delivered volume
Minimize manual reconciliation effort per settlement cycle
Eliminate payment disputes caused by identifier or timestamp mismatch, as opposed to genuine under-performance
researchGaps: What share of flexibility payment disputes are caused by identifier/timestamp mismatch vs. genuine under-performance?
Do industrial sites actively dispute payments or accept haircuts passively?
Are any market operators already providing standardized SCADA-to-settlement reconciliation tooling?

linkedIdeas.ideaName: FlexCovenant -- Industrial Flexibility Performance Contract OS
linkedIdeas.residualProblem: FlexCovenant addresses the reconciliation and payment verification layer. It does not address the underlying architectural issue that industrial sites lack direct access to grid operator settlement data (step-flex-07) — which is a regulatory/access problem requiring grid operator or regulator participation. Aggregators would need to integrate with or expose FlexCovenant data for sites to independently verify.

problems.title: B2B buyers cannot access independent product performance evidence before purchase — all available evidence is vendor-controlled
problems.description: When evaluating complex or specialized products and services, B2B buyers have access almost exclusively to vendor-curated evidence: vendor-selected case studies, vendor-briefed reference customers, and vendor-produced certification documents. No neutral repository of independent test results at the configuration level a specific buyer needs exists for most product categories. As a result, buyers must either run expensive proof-of-concept tests themselves, rely on vendor-selected references, or accept residual uncertainty at purchase time. Gaps between claimed and actual performance are commonly discovered post-contract.

actors.organizationType: B2B buyer organization (any sector with high-stakes vendor selection)

jobs.statement: Independently verify that a vendor's product or service performs as claimed before committing to a purchase or contract.

workflowSummary.name: B2B Vendor Product Claim Verification During Procurement
workflowSummary.trigger: A B2B buyer needs to evaluate a vendor's product or service for purchase. Vendor has made performance, compatibility, or certification claims.
workflowSummary.goal: Buyer has sufficient independent evidence to make a confident, defensible purchase decision.

steps.action: Identify evaluation criteria and gather vendor-provided materials (datasheets, white papers, case studies, certifications).
Assess whether vendor-provided evidence is independent or self-reported. Request third-party test results, certifications, or reference customers.
steps.output: List of evidence gaps and requests
steps.frictionNotes: All evidence provided by vendor is vendor-selected. Certification documents may be real but may not match buyer's specific configuration (different voltage, jurisdiction, use case).

steps.action: Contact vendor-provided reference customers. Conduct reference calls.
steps.duration: 1–3 weeks to arrange; 30–60 min per reference
steps.frictionNotes: Vendor curates reference list — only satisfied customers included. References may be briefed. Buyer cannot contact non-reference customers. Reference experience may not match buyer's use case.

steps.action: Attempt own proof-of-concept or pilot test in buyer's specific environment (if feasible).
steps.frictionNotes: Expensive (internal time, setup cost). Not always feasible for complex or regulated products. May require NDA, separate contract, IT approval. Pilot may not replicate production conditions.

steps.action: Make purchase decision with available evidence, accepting residual uncertainty, or reject vendor.
steps.frictionNotes: Buyer typically accepts vendor claims partially on faith, especially for novel or specialized products with no independent test data available.

steps.action: Post-purchase: discover that actual performance does not match claimed performance in specific configuration.
steps.frictionNotes: Post-contract discovery of gaps is expensive to remediate (replacement, renegotiation, legal). Occurs because pre-purchase evidence was insufficient for buyer's specific conditions.

frictions.description: All available pre-purchase evidence is vendor-controlled. Buyer cannot access evidence from non-reference customers.
No neutral source of independent product performance data at the configuration level a specific buyer needs.
Running an independent pilot/PoC in buyer's environment is expensive and slow; often 2–12 weeks and significant internal resource.

workarounds.description: Buyers rely on vendor-curated reference calls with pre-selected satisfied customers.
workarounds.limitations: Vendor controls who is on the reference list. Does not surface neutral or negative experiences.

workarounds.description: Buyers run their own proof-of-concept tests in their own environment.
workarounds.cost: 2–12 weeks staff time, setup cost, potential pilot license fee
workarounds.limitations: Not feasible for all product categories. Expensive. May still not resolve all configuration-specific questions.

contexts: High-stakes B2B procurement (capital equipment, B2B SaaS, regulated materials, certified components)
Novel or specialized product categories with no established independent benchmarks
Regulated industries where certification specifics matter for compliance

evidence.summary: Reconstructed from FactBounty (idea-061) dossier. The structural information asymmetry between vendor-controlled evidence and buyer need for independent evidence is the core thesis. Real buyer interviews needed to quantify severity and frequency.

counterEvidence.summary: For widely-deployed software products, review platforms (G2, Gartner Peer Insights) already provide substantial independent user evidence. The problem may be most acute for niche, industrial, or regulated products without mainstream review coverage.

Large enterprise buyers (Fortune 500) typically have procurement teams that run extensive RFP processes, independent testing labs, and industry analyst relationships that partially address this gap. The problem may be proportionally more severe for mid-market buyers.

In some regulated industries (pharmaceutical, aerospace), third-party certification bodies already provide structured independent product qualification. This existing infrastructure could mean the problem is lower-severity in those verticals.

currentWorkarounds: Vendor-selected reference calls (biased toward satisfied customers)
Internal proof-of-concept testing (expensive and slow, 2–12 weeks)
Public review sites (G2, Capterra, Gartner Peer Insights) — useful for some SaaS, absent for industrial/regulated products
Peer-network inquiries through professional associations or LinkedIn
consequences: Buyers make purchase decisions with higher residual uncertainty than desired
Post-contract performance gaps discovered too late to avoid remediation cost (replacement, renegotiation, legal)
Buyers spend weeks on reference calls that are structurally biased toward vendor-favorable outcomes
Smaller buyers (without resources for full PoC) are more exposed than large enterprise buyers
desiredOutcomes: Access independent evidence of product performance in configurations similar to buyer's own environment, before purchase commitment
Reduce time and cost of vendor evaluation for high-stakes purchases
Reduce post-contract surprise rate from gaps between claimed and actual performance
researchGaps: What share of B2B purchase decisions include an independent PoC step vs. relying on references/certifications alone?
Which product categories have the widest gap between available independent evidence and buyer needs?
How often do post-contract performance gaps result in formal disputes vs. silent acceptance?
Would buyers pay for access to independent evidence from comparable buyers? (Demand-side willingness.)

linkedIdeas.residualProblem: FactBounty targets the supply side of the evidence asymmetry — creating a marketplace for buyer-funded product proof. However, it does not address the step-vv-04 (in-buyer-environment PoC) friction where buyers need evidence specific to their own technical configuration. Marketplace-sourced evidence may still come from different use cases or configurations than the buyer's own context. Additionally, bootstrapping a two-sided marketplace from zero requires achieving critical mass of both buyers and product testers — a significant cold-start problem.
